ladders.base: This paper presents a method for multi-class classification using a "pairwise" neural network architecture, where a K-class problem is decomposed into K(K−1)/2 two-class sub-problems, each handled by a small neural network (potentially a single sigmoidal neuron) trained only on data from its respective pair of classes. Since raw two-class network outputs are not necessarily calibrated probabilities for real-world (non-Gaussian) data, the authors convert them to probabilities in two steps: first, class-conditional densities over each network's linear output are estimated (e.g., by fitting Gaussians) and transformed into pairwise posterior probabilities via Bayes' rule, under the assumption that the network output is as informative as the input; second, these pairwise probabilities are combined using a closed-form expression derived from the inclusion–exclusion principle to yield posterior probabilities for all K classes. The approach is applied to recognizing pre-segmented characters from cursive handwriting on French postal checks (27 classes, ~55,000 characters), where it achieves competitive recognition performance compared to multilayer perceptrons trained with backpropagation or Softmax—though Softmax scored highest in raw accuracy, the pairwise classifier trains over an order of magnitude faster, allows incremental updates when classes change, and offers greater insight into the classification problem. Integrated into a complete check-reading system with word-level post-processing, the method contributed to recognizing 80% of checks correctly at a 1% error rate.

ladders.base: The paper proposes a scalable way to obtain calibrated, multi-class posterior probabilities by decomposing a K-class problem into K(K−1)/2 two-class neural networks and then recombining their outputs. Each pairwise network is a small classifier trained only on two classes; to make its single output probabilistic, the authors fit class-conditional densities to the network’s linear output (before the sigmoid), apply Bayes’ rule to compute pairwise posteriors Prij, and then derive full K-class posteriors via a closed-form combination that uses all pairwise probabilities, avoiding brittle selection of (K−1) pairs required by alternatives. Applied to real-world cursive handwriting recognition on French postal checks with 27 classes (including frequent letter pairs), the system normalizes segmented characters, trains 351 single-neuron pairwise classifiers, models the linear outputs as Gaussians, and aggregates probabilities for use by word-level decoding (e.g., Edit Distance). On a 55k-character dataset, the pairwise method achieves 48.9% top-1 with equal priors (52.2% with true priors) and fast training; a Softmax MLP attains higher accuracy (54.9%/61.9%) but at significantly greater computational cost. Integrated into a full check-reading pipeline, the approach yields 83.3% top-1 word accuracy, 64.1% correct literal amounts, and 80% correctly read checks at 1% error, while offering practical advantages: rapid experimentation, easy class addition, and diagnostic insight into class confusions.

ladders.base: This paper presents a method for obtaining posterior class probabilities from a pairwise (one-vs-one) neural network classifier for K-class problems, where K(K−1)/2 small networks are each trained to discriminate a pair of classes. For each pairwise network, the authors fit Gaussians to the class-conditional densities of the single output neuron's pre-activation, apply Bayes' rule to get pairwise posteriors Pr(ω_i | ω_ij, x), then derive a closed-form expression combining all pairwise probabilities into the K class posteriors: Pr(ω_i|x) = 1 / (Σ_{j≠i} 1/Pr_ij − (K−2)). This improves on an earlier method (Refregier & Vallet) that required selecting an optimal subset of K−1 pairwise probabilities per pattern. The approach is applied to recognizing pre-segmented characters (27 classes) from cursive handwriting on French postal checks, using single sigmoidal neurons as the pairwise classifiers on 10×24 pixel inputs. Compared to MLPs trained with backpropagation or Softmax and to 27 one-vs-all MLPs, the pairwise classifier's raw accuracy (~52% top-1) is somewhat below Softmax MLPs (~62%), but it trains over an order of magnitude faster, allows incremental addition of classes without full retraining, and yields interpretable pairwise structure; integrated into a full check-reading system it contributes to 80% correct check recognition at 1% error.

For each pair of classes, a single-neuron classifier is trained, and its linear output is modeled using class-conditional probability density estimation (fitted to Gaussians) to compute pairwise posterior probabilities via Bayes' rule. These pairwise estimates are then analytically combined via an exact probability-of-union formulation into global posterior class probabilities: $\operatorname{Pr}(\omega_i \mid x) = \left[\sum_{j \neq i} \operatorname{Pr}_{ij}^{-1} - (K-2)\right]^{-1}$. Evaluated on a 27-class cursive character recognition task for French postal check reading (comprising ~55,000 pre-segmented character images), the pairwise classifier achieved a 48.9% first-position accuracy under equal priors (average rank 2.9) and 52.2% under true priors (average rank 2.6). Although standard Softmax MLPs attained slightly higher accuracy (54.9% and 61.9%, respectively), the pairwise architecture offers practical advantages, including more than an order-of-magnitude faster training, modularity for adding or modifying classes without full retraining, and seamless integration with downstream dynamic programming algorithms like Edit Distance for cursive word recognition.
